paragraphs.text: Observed and Projected Precipitation Extremes over Phetchaburi Province under CMIP6 SSP Scenarios
Surasit Punyawansiri 1,*
1Office of Water Management and Hydrology, Royal Irrigation Department, Dusit, Bangkok 10300, Thailand
*Corresponding author: Surasit.pu@ku.th
Abstract

Changes in precipitation extremes can occur alongside shifts in rainfall totals, wet and dry spells, and event intensity, creating competing signals for water-resource planning. This study assessed observed trends and near-term projected changes in 11 annual precipitation-extreme indices at 13 rain gauges in Phetchaburi Province, Thailand. Daily observations for 1981–2014 were analyzed using the two-sided Mann–Kendall test and Sen’s slope estimator, with Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate control applied to 143 station–index tests. The Yue–Wang effective-sample-size adjustment was used as a sensitivity diagnostic. Future changes for 2021–2050 were estimated from seven supplied bias-corrected CMIP6 models under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 relative to each model’s 1995–2014 baseline. A model-first approach calculated the station median within each model before summarizing the seven model-level changes. Observations showed significant decreases in PRCPTOT and CWD at 9 and 11 stations, respectively, and increases in CDD, SDII, Rx1day, R95p, and R99p at 10, 9, 7, 8, and 9 stations, respectively; 88 of 143 tests remained significant after false-discovery-rate control. Median PRCPTOT changes were −2.5% under SSP2-4.5 and −9.0% under SSP5-8.5, whereas R99p increased by 59.0% and 20.1%, respectively, with substantial inter-model spread. Station-referenced IDW indicated broader negative PRCPTOT changes under SSP5-8.5 but represents spatial depiction rather than validated gridded projection. Overall, the results indicate declining wet-day totals and longer dry spells in observations, while future changes remain model- and scenario-dependent.
Keywords: Climate change, Precipitation extremes, Mann–Kendall test, Sen’s slope, Phetchaburi Province
1. Introduction

Precipitation extremes are an important consequence of a warming climate, with implications for water-supply reliability, agricultural productivity, flood risk, and community resilience [1,2]. The hydroclimatic response to global warming is not necessarily expressed as a uniform change in annual precipitation totals; rather, precipitation characteristics are influenced by thermodynamic effects associated with increased atmospheric moisture capacity and by regional dynamical processes, including monsoon variability, convection, and land–sea thermal contrasts [1,2]. Consequently, a region may experience more intense precipitation events alongside longer dry spells, reflecting changes in the temporal distribution of precipitation [1,2]. Capturing these contrasting characteristics therefore benefits from a suite of complementary duration-, intensity-, frequency-, and percentile-based precipitation-extreme indices rather than a single aggregate rainfall metric [2].

The Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) provides a coordinated framework for evaluating climate-model responses, with ScenarioMIP providing scenario-based projections under pathways such as SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 [3-5]. Regional assessments, however, remain subject to structural model uncertainty and sensitivity of precipitation extremes to bias-correction choices [6,7]. Regional studies also show substantial inter-model spread and, for some indices, differences in the direction of projected change across models [6,7]. These findings support an index-by-index assessment with explicit baselines, transparent aggregation, and explicit characterization of inter-model spread.

Across Thailand, recent studies have documented non-stationary rainfall variability, historical trends, and projected changes in precipitation extremes across northern, central, and southern regions [8-12], as well as nationwide shifts toward intensified daily rainfall regimes [13]. However, station-level assessments integrating multiple ETCCDI-family indices, observed trends, and CMIP6 scenario changes remain limited for Phetchaburi Province. Phetchaburi is an important agricultural and water-resource area in the Phetchaburi–Prachuap Khiri Khan region, where localized evidence on precipitation extremes can support flood-risk assessment and water-resource planning [8,12].

To address this gap, this study examines 11 ETCCDI-family precipitation-extreme indices using observations from 13 rain gauges in Phetchaburi Province and evaluates projected changes from seven CMIP6 models under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. The analysis focuses on three questions: (i) which precipitation-extreme indices showed significant trends during 1981–2014; (ii) how projected changes during 2021–2050 vary among the seven CMIP6 models relative to the 1995–2014 baseline; and (iii) what broad spatial contrasts are suggested by the station-referenced projections across the province. The findings provide localized evidence relevant to flood-risk assessment and water-resource planning in Phetchaburi Province.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1 Study area, observations and model series

The study area is Phetchaburi Province, Thailand. Daily precipitation observations for 1981–2014 were obtained from 13 meteorological stations (Figure 1; Table 1). The supplied model dataset comprises daily historical and scenario precipitation series from the seven CMIP6 GCMs listed in Table 2. Historical model output was summarized over 1995–2014 as the baseline period, and future projections were evaluated for 2021–2050. The 1995–2014 period was selected as the baseline because it is the AR6 recent-past reference period used for assessing future climate projections, and 2014 is the final year of the CMIP6 historical simulations [1].

2.2 Annual precipitation indices and quality control

We calculated 11 annual precipitation-extreme indices from the ETCCDI family (Table 3): PRCPTOT (wet-day precipitation total), SDII (wet-day mean intensity), Rx1day and Rx5day (annual one- and five-day maxima), CDD and CWD (maximum consecutive dry and wet days), R10mm, R20mm and R50mm (counts of days at or above 10, 20 and 50 mm), and R95p and R99p (annual precipitation above station-specific 95th and 99th wet-day thresholds). A wet day was RR ≥ 1 mm. The percentile thresholds were fixed once from each station’s complete 1981–2014 wet-day distribution; they were not re-estimated separately in each year or future window. Accordingly, R95p and R99p are treated here as fixed-reference percentile indices; their implementation should not be assumed to be identical to that of every ETCCDI software package [2,14].
Table 3. Definitions of extreme precipitation indices used in the study.
Notes: A wet day is RR ≥ 1 mm. R95p and R99p use station-specific fixed wet-day thresholds estimated from 1981–2014 and retained for all annual and future-window calculations.

The analysis used the Gregorian calendar for observations. CanESM5, CESM2 and FGOALS-g3 use a 365-day no-leap calendar; February 29 is therefore absent from these model series and was not imputed. Annual completeness was evaluated using the applicable model calendar. Annual summaries required at least 90% valid daily records. A missing day was not silently converted to zero; it interrupted spells and moving windows. The minimum annual completeness across model records was 99.73%.
2.3 Trend inference and multiple testing

Trend detection for the historical observations and the within-window future diagnostic was performed using the standard two-sided Mann–Kendall (MK) test [15] with Sen’s slope estimator [16]. 2.5 Station-referenced IDW mapping
Inverse-distance weighting (IDW), a deterministic interpolator for irregularly spaced observations [20], was used to depict broad spatial contrast. For a map location x, the displayed field was:

These maps are descriptive spatial depictions of station-referenced changes and are not interpreted as dynamically downscaled or independently validated gridded projections. Areas outside the station convex hull are treated as spatial extrapolation.
3. Results
3.1 Data completeness and observed trends

The final run produced 4,862 station-year index records, 143 observed trend rows, 60,060 future index records, 2,002 future trend rows and 2,002 future-change rows. The observed 95th-percentile thresholds ranged from 14.5 to 42.8 mm and the 99th-percentile thresholds from 26.6 to 76.448 mm, confirming that a common provincial threshold would have removed substantial local intensity contrast.

The dominant observed signal was a decline in wet-day precipitation totals and wet-spell duration, accompanied by increases in dry-spell duration and wet-day intensity (Table 4; Figure 2). Standard MK identified 93 of 143 tests as significant; after BH-FDR control, 88 remained significant. PRCPTOT showed significant decreases at nine stations in the primary MK analysis, with a median Sen slope of −164.88 mm per decade. CWD decreased at 11 stations (median −27.04 days per decade), whereas CDD increased at 10 stations (median +9.23 days per decade). SDII increased at nine stations (median +0.54 mm day−1 per decade), and Rx1day, R95p and R99p increased at seven, eight and nine stations, respectively, in the primary test. Rx5day showed weaker spatial coherence, with only two significant decreases, and R50mm had five increases, one decrease and six non-significant station results.

3.2 Near-term model changes

The model-first results indicate a mixed projected response rather than a uniform provincial shift (Table 5; Figure 3). Under SSP2-4.5, the median PRCPTOT change was −2.5% (IQR, −6.5% to +8.0%), while the corresponding medians for Rx1day, Rx5day, R95p, and R99p were +4.8%, +7.6%, +9.6%, and +59.0%, respectively. The wide R99p range is consistent with substantial inter-model spread and with the sensitivity of relative changes to small baseline values for this extreme-tail index. CDD and CWD had median changes of −8.3% and −9.0%, respectively; however, the model range for CDD crossed zero, while that for CWD remained broad. Importantly, the pronounced inter-model spread, particularly for upper-tail and threshold indices such as R50mm, R95p, and R99p, indicates that projected changes are strongly model-dependent and should not be interpreted as a single deterministic provincial signal.

Under SSP5-8.5, the median PRCPTOT change was −9.0% (IQR −15.0 to +1.2%). R10mm had a median decrease of 9.6% and CWD by −7.2%, whereas R20mm increased by 2.7% and R99p by +20.1%; the corresponding IQRs crossed zero for most indices. The seven-model sign counts show this uncertainty directly: for PRCPTOT, SSP2-4.5 produced three positive and four negative model medians, while SSP5-8.5 produced two positive and five negative medians. The contrast is therefore stronger for the total-rainfall signal under SSP5-8.5 than for the tail indices. R50mm is a count index with low event frequency; its large relative percentages (for example, an SSP2-4.5 median of +33.3% with a model range of −33.3 to +300.0%) are unstable when baseline counts are small and should therefore not be treated as a headline climate signal.

3.3 Within-window trend diagnostics

The 30-year future-window standard MK diagnostic identified significant trends in 56 of 1,001 SSP2-4.5 model–station–index series (45 increasing and 11 decreasing) and 76 of 1,001 SSP5-8.5 series (5 increasing and 71 decreasing). These unadjusted counts do not establish field significance and are not interchangeable with the model-first mean changes. They are retained as a temporal diagnostic: a model can show a negative 2021–2050 slope even when its future mean is above the 1995–2014 baseline, and vice versa. This separation is important for avoiding the common conflation of projected level change with a monotonic trend within a short window.
3.4 Spatial depiction of PRCPTOT change

The IDW fields provide a spatial depiction of the station-referenced model-median PRCPTOT changes (Figure 4). Under SSP2-4.5, the northern and central areas are close to neutral or weakly positive, whereas the southern and southeastern station cluster shows more negative changes. Under SSP5-8.5, negative changes are more spatially extensive across the province. These patterns represent spatial interpolation of station-referenced projected changes and should not be interpreted as continuous-resolution climate projections between gauges.

Figure 4. Spatial distribution of projected changes in annual precipitation total (PRCPTOT) over Phetchaburi Province for 2021–2050 relative to 1995–2014 under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. (a) SSP2-4.5; (b) SSP5-8.5.
4. Discussion
4.1 Declining wet-day precipitation totals and stronger daily intensity

The observed Phetchaburi pattern combines lower wet-day precipitation totals and shorter wet spells with longer dry spells and greater wet-day intensity. This combination suggests a redistribution of precipitation characteristics between wet-day occurrence and intensity, although the station-based analysis does not identify the underlying atmospheric mechanism. These results indicate changes in the distribution of precipitation rather than a uniform increase across all heavy-precipitation indices and stations. The station-level matrix in Figure 2 shows less spatial coherence for Rx5day and R50mm than for Rx1day, R95p, and R99p; this pattern may be influenced by the greater variability associated with multi-day extremes and high-threshold event counts.

The direction of the historical signal is broadly consistent with Thai studies reporting non-stationary rainfall variability, spatially heterogeneous trends, and changes in extreme-event frequency [9-12,21]. These regional findings should not, however, be transferred directly to Phetchaburi. Differences in the gauge network, observation period, and percentile-threshold definition mean that the present study targets a different estimand. Likewise, the Cyprus study’s finding that model rankings and the direction of index changes vary by period and scenario provides a useful methodological comparison, but it is not evidence of a Phetchaburi-specific mechanism [7].
4.2 Scenario dependence and inter-model spread

The projected changes during 2021–2050 indicate substantial scenario dependence and inter-model spread. The median PRCPTOT change was more negative under SSP5-8.5 (−9.0%) than under SSP2-4.5 (−2.5%), although the IQR under SSP5-8.5 still included zero. The upper-tail indices show a contrasting pattern: R99p has a positive median change under both scenarios, but its model range is wide. Relative changes in tail indices can be sensitive to small baseline values, limited event counts, and the characteristics of the supplied bias-corrected series. Previous studies have shown that bias correction may improve distributional agreement while altering temporal dependence and event sequencing; therefore, its suitability should be evaluated for the specific extreme metric of interest rather than assumed to be neutral preprocessing [22-25].

The broad inter-model spread provides important context for interpreting the projected changes. Because CMIP6 models are not independent random draws, the seven-model median should be interpreted as a descriptive measure of central tendency rather than as a calibrated probability estimate. Recent assessments of CMIP6 model selection, statistical downscaling, and artificial-intelligence downscaling likewise emphasize that model skill and methodological choices can influence the local projected signal [14,24-30]. The model-first aggregation reduces the influence of unequal station representation on the ensemble summary but does not eliminate structural differences among models or uncertainty associated with scenario choice. The ensemble summaries indicate a tendency toward lower wet-day precipitation totals under SSP5-8.5, whereas several upper-tail indices show positive median changes accompanied by substantial inter-model spread.
4.3 Statistical and spatial limitations

Three main limitations constrain the interpretation of these results. First, the 1981–2014 observational record spans 34 years, limiting the effective sample size for extreme-tail analysis. The 30-year within-window trend diagnostics are likewise sensitive to sampling variability. Standard MK/Sen is reported as the primary reproducible analysis, while Yue–Wang is used as a sensitivity diagnostic; the two can yield different results when autocorrelation alters the variance estimate. Second, BH-FDR is applied to the 143 observed station–index tests but not to the unadjusted within-window future diagnostic, which is used only for descriptive purposes. Third, IDW provides a spatial depiction of station-referenced values. It cannot recover topographic or coastal gradients that are not represented by the station network and may extrapolate outside the station convex hull. The resulting surface depends on station density and boundary geometry [20]. It should therefore be interpreted as a depiction of broad spatial contrasts rather than as evidence of unsupported fine-scale gradients.
5. Conclusion

Phetchaburi observations showed declining wet-day precipitation totals and wet-spell duration, alongside longer dry spells and increases in wet-day intensity and several upper-tail indices. PRCPTOT and CWD had median Sen’s slopes of −164.88 mm decade⁻¹ and −27.04 days decade⁻¹, respectively, while 88 of 143 observed station–index tests remained significant after Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate control. The Yue–Wang adjustment provided a sensitivity check for serial correlation rather than an alternative primary inference. Projected changes during 2021–2050 showed substantial inter-model and scenario dependence. The median PRCPTOT change was −2.5% under SSP2-4.5 and −9.0% under SSP5-8.5, whereas R99p increased by 59.0% and 20.1%, respectively, with wide inter-model spread. Rx5day and R50mm were less spatially coherent or more sensitive to small event counts. Overall, the results indicate a combination of lower wet-day precipitation totals, longer dry spells, and stronger precipitation extremes at many stations, highlighting the need to consider both flood and water-resource risks in regional planning.

package.all_xml_text: Observed and Projected Precipitation Extremes over Phetchaburi Province under CMIP6 SSP Scenarios Surasit Punyawansiri 1,* 1 Office of Water Management and Hydrology, Royal Irrigation Department, Dusit, Bangkok 10300, Thailand *Corresponding author: Surasit.pu@ku.th Abstract Changes in precipitation extremes can occur alongside shifts in rainfall totals, wet and dry spells, and event intensity, creating competing signals for water-resource planning. This study assessed observed trends and near-term projected changes in 11 annual precipitation-extreme indices at 13 rain gauges in Phetchaburi Province, Thailand. Daily observations for 1981–2014 were analyzed using the two-sided Mann–Kendall test and Sen’s slope estimator, with Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate control applied to 143 station–index tests. The Yue–Wang effective-sample-size adjustment was used as a sensitivity diagnostic. Future changes for 2021–2050 were estimated from seven supplied bias-corrected CMIP6 models under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 relative to each model’s 1995–2014 baseline. A model-first approach calculated the station median within each model before summarizing the seven model-level changes. Observations showed significant decreases in PRCPTOT and CWD at 9 and 11 stations, respectively, and increases in CDD, SDII, Rx1day, R95p, and R99p at 10, 9, 7, 8, and 9 stations, respectively; 88 of 143 tests remained significant after false-discovery-rate control. Median PRCPTOT changes were −2.5% under SSP2-4.5 and −9.0% under SSP5-8.5, whereas R99p increased by 59.0% and 20.1%, respectively, with substantial inter-model spread. Station-referenced IDW indicated broader negative PRCPTOT changes under SSP5-8.5 but represents spatial depiction rather than validated gridded projection. Overall, the results indicate declining wet-day totals and longer dry spells in observations, while future changes remain model- and scenario-dependent. Keywords: Climate change, P recipitation extremes , Mann–Kendall test, Sen’s slope, Phetchaburi Province 1. Introduction Precipitation extremes are an important consequence of a warming climate, with implications for water-supply reliability, agricultural productivity, flood risk, and community resilience [1,2]. The hydroclimatic response to global warming is not necessarily expressed as a uniform change in annual precipitation totals; rather, precipitation characteristics are influenced by thermodynamic effects associated with increased atmospheric moisture capacity and by regional dynamical processes, including monsoon variability, convection, and land–sea thermal contrasts [1,2]. Consequently, a region may experience more intense precipitation events alongside longer dry spells, reflecting changes in the temporal distribution of precipitation [1,2]. Capturing these contrasting characteristics therefore benefits from a suite of complementary duration-, intensity-, frequency-, and percentile-based precipitation-extreme indices rather than a single aggregate rainfall metric [2] . The Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) provides a coordinated framework for evaluating climate-model responses, with ScenarioMIP providing scenario-based projections under pathways such as SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 [3 - 5]. Regional assessments, however, remain subject to structural model uncertainty and sensitivity of precipitation extremes to bias-correction choices [6,7]. Regional studies also show substantial inter-model spread and, for some indices, differences in the direction of projected change across models [6,7]. These findings support an index-by-index assessment with explicit baselines, transparent aggregation, and explicit characterization of inter-model spread . Across Thailand, recent studies have documented non-stationary rainfall variability, historical trends, and projected changes in precipitation extremes across northern, central, and southern regions [8-12], as well as nationwide shifts toward intensified daily rainfall regimes [13]. However, station-level assessments integrating multiple ETCCDI-family indices, observed trends, and CMIP6 scenario changes remain limited for Phetchaburi Province . Phetchaburi is an important agricultural and water-resource area in the Phetchaburi–Prachuap Khiri Khan region, where localized evidence on precipitation extremes can support flood-risk assessment and water-resource planning [ 8 , 1 2]. To address this gap, this study examines 11 ETCCDI-family precipitation-extreme indices using observations from 13 rain gauges in Phetchaburi Province and evaluates projected changes from seven CMIP6 models under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. The analysis focuses on three questions: ( i ) which precipitation-extreme indices showed significant trends during 1981–2014; (ii) how projected changes during 2021–2050 vary among the seven CMIP6 models relative to the 1995–2014 baseline; and (iii) what broad spatial contrasts are suggested by the station-referenced projections across the province. The findings provide localized evidence relevant to flood-risk assessment and water-resource planning in Phetchaburi Province . 2. Materials and Methods 2.1 Study area, observations and model series The study area is Phetchaburi Province, Thailand. Daily precipitation observations for 1981–2014 were obtained from 13 meteorological stations (Figure 1; Table 1). The supplied model dataset comprises daily historical and scenario precipitation series from the seven CMIP6 GCMs listed in Table 2. Historical model output was summarized over 1995–2014 as the baseline period, and future projections were evaluated for 2021–2050. The 1995–2014 period was selected as the baseline because it is the AR6 recent-past reference period used for assessing future climate projections, and 2014 is the final year of the CMIP6 historical simulations [ 1 ]. Discussion 4.1 Declining wet-day precipitation totals and stronger daily intensity The observed Phetchaburi pattern combines lower wet-day precipitation totals and shorter wet spells with longer dry spells and greater wet-day intensity. This combination suggests a redistribution of precipitation characteristics between wet-day occurrence and intensity, although the station-based analysis does not identify the underlying atmospheric mechanism. These results indicate changes in the distribution of precipitation rather than a uniform increase across all heavy-precipitation indices and stations. The station-level matrix in Figure 2 shows less spatial coherence for Rx5day and R50mm than for Rx1day, R95p, and R99p; this pattern may be influenced by the greater variability associated with multi-day extremes and high-threshold event counts. The direction of the historical signal is broadly consistent with Thai studies reporting non-stationary rainfall variability, spatially heterogeneous trends, and changes in extreme-event frequency [ 9-12,21 ]. These regional findings should not, however, be transferred directly to Phetchaburi. Differences in the gauge network, observation period, and percentile-threshold definition mean that the present study targets a different estimand . Likewise, the Cyprus study’s finding that model rankings and the direction of index changes vary by period and scenario provides a useful methodological comparison, but it is not evidence of a Phetchaburi-specific mechanism [7]. 4.2 Scenario dependence and inter-model spread The projected changes during 2021–2050 indicate substantial scenario dependence and inter-model spread. The median PRCPTOT change was more negative under SSP5-8.5 (−9.0%) than under SSP2-4.5 (−2.5%), although the IQR under SSP5-8.5 still included zero. The upper-tail indices show a contrasting pattern: R99p has a positive median change under both scenarios, but its model range is wide. Relative changes in tail indices can be sensitive to small baseline values, limited event counts, and the characteristics of the supplied bias-corrected series. Previous studies have shown that bias correction may improve distributional agreement while altering temporal dependence and event sequencing; therefore, its suitability should be evaluated for the specific extreme metric of interest rather than assumed to be neutral preprocessing [ 22-25 ]. The broad inter-model spread provides important context for interpreting the projected changes. Because CMIP6 models are not independent random draws, the seven-model median should be interpreted as a descriptive measure of central tendency rather than as a calibrated probability estimate. Recent assessments of CMIP6 model selection, statistical downscaling, and artificial-intelligence downscaling likewise emphasize that model skill and methodological choices can influence the local projected signal [ 14,24- 30 ]. The model-first aggregation reduces the influence of unequal station representation on the ensemble summary but does not eliminate structural differences among models or uncertainty associated with scenario choice. The ensemble summaries indicate a tendency toward lower wet-day precipitation totals under SSP5-8.5, whereas several upper-tail indices show positive median changes accompanied by substantial inter-model spread . 4.3 Statistical and spatial limitations Three main limitations constrain the interpretation of these results. First, the 1981–2014 observational record spans 34 years, limiting the effective sample size for extreme-tail analysis. The 30-year within-window trend diagnostics are likewise sensitive to sampling variability. Standard MK/Sen is reported as the primary reproducible analysis, while Yue–Wang is used as a sensitivity diagnostic; the two can yield different results when autocorrelation alters the variance estimate. Second, BH-FDR is applied to the 143 observed station–index tests but not to the unadjusted within-window future diagnostic, which is used only for descriptive purposes. Third, IDW provides a spatial depiction of station-referenced values. It cannot recover topographic or coastal gradients that are not represented by the station network and may extrapolate outside the station convex hull. The resulting surface depends on station density and boundary geometry [ 20 ]. It should therefore be interpreted as a depiction of broad spatial contrasts rather than as evidence of unsupported fine-scale gradients. 5. Conclusion Phetchaburi observations showed declining wet-day precipitation totals and wet-spell duration, alongside longer dry spells and increases in wet-day intensity and several upper-tail indices. PRCPTOT and CWD had median Sen’s slopes of −164.88 mm decade⁻¹ and −27.04 days decade⁻¹, respectively, while 88 of 143 observed station–index tests remained significant after Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate control. The Yue–Wang adjustment provided a sensitivity check for serial correlation rather than an alternative primary inference. Projected changes during 2021–2050 showed substantial inter-model and scenario dependence. The median PRCPTOT change was −2.5% under SSP2-4.5 and −9.0% under SSP5-8.5, whereas R99p increased by 59.0% and 20.1%, respectively, with wide inter-model spread. Rx5day and R50mm were less spatially coherent or more sensitive to small event counts. Overall, the results indicate a combination of lower wet-day precipitation totals, longer dry spells, and stronger precipitation extremes at many stations, highlighting the need to consider both flood and water-resource risks in regional planning. 6.
